title: DEIM: DETR with Improved Matching for Fast Convergence

problem.summary: DETR-style detectors converge slowly because one-to-one Hungarian matching yields only one positive sample per target (sparse supervision) and randomly initialized queries produce many low-quality matches that existing losses barely optimize.
statements: One-to-one matching assigns only one positive sample per target, far fewer than one-to-many assignment, so supervision is sparse and training is slow.
DETR's small set of randomly initialized queries lacks spatial alignment with targets, causing matches with low IoU but high confidence scores.
YOLO-style one-to-many training needs hand-crafted NMS to remove overlapping boxes, which adds latency and instability.

evidence.quote: However, slow convergence remains one of the primary limitations of DETRs, and we hypothesize that the reasons are two-fold.
Sparse supervision: The O2O matching mechanism assigns only one positive sample per target, greatly limiting the number of positive samples.
Unlike traditional methods that rely on dense anchors (usually > 8000), DETR employs a small number (100 or 300) of randomly initialized queries.
However, it produces multiple overlapping bounding boxes per object, requiring a hand-crafted Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) to remove redundancies, introducing latency and instability [32, 43].

background.summary: The paper builds on DETR/Hungarian one-to-one matching, on prior O2M-assisted DETR training (Group DETR, Co-DETR, H-DETR) that adds decoders, on query-initialization work (DN-DETR, DINO, RT-DETR), and on Varifocal Loss as used by RT-DETR, plus the real-time DETR lineage RT-DETR and D-FINE.

relatedWork.name: Group DETR / Co-DETR
relatedWork.relation: prior ways to add positive samples inside O2O training, but with extra decoders/heads
relatedWork.quote: Although these approaches successfully increase the number of positive samples, they also require additional decoders, which increases computational overhead and risks generating redundant high-quality predictions as traditional detectors.

relatedWork.name: Varifocal Loss (VFL)
relatedWork.relation: the loss DEIM modifies; designed for dense anchors and high-IoU matches
relatedWork.quote: Existing loss functions [19, 40] in DETRs, such as Varifocal Loss (VFL) [40], are tailored to dense anchors where the number of low-quality matches is relatively low.

relatedWork.name: RT-DETR
relatedWork.relation: real-time DETR baseline and host framework for DEIM
relatedWork.quote: RT-DETR is the first real-time object detection model within the DETR framework.

relatedWork.name: D-FINE
relatedWork.relation: the detector that DEIM boosts to its headline numbers
relatedWork.quote: This approach enables D-FINE to achieve a more favorable trade-off between latency and performance, slightly surpassing recent YOLO models.

evidence.quote: adopt a one-to-one (O2O) matching strategy that leverages the Hungarian [16] algorithm to establish a unique correspondence between predicted boxes and the ground-truth objects during training, eliminating the need for NMS.

solution.summary: DEIM is a training framework combining Dense O2O matching, which multiplies targets per image via mosaic/mixup so one-to-one matching gets dense supervision, with a Matchability-Aware Loss (MAL) that weights positives by IoU-quality to fix low-quality matches, all without extra decoders or added inference cost.
solution.approach: Increase the number of targets per training image (Dense O2O) to densify positive samples, and use MAL (a VFL variant whose positive target is q^gamma) so low-quality matches are optimized too.
components: Dense O2O matching: mosaic and mixup augmentations multiply targets per image while keeping Mi = 1
Matchability-Aware Loss (MAL) combining IoU quality with classification confidence
DataAug Warmup scheduler that disables advanced augmentation in early epochs
Optionally disable Dense O2O after 50% of training epochs

evidence.quote: We propose Dense O2O as an efficient alternative. This strategy retains the one-to-one matching structure of O2O (with Mi = 1), but increases the number of targets (N ) per image, achieving denser supervision.

this can be easily achieved using classical techniques such as mosaic [1] and mixup [38] augmentations, which generates additional positive samples per image while preserving the one-to-one matching framework.
MAL scales the penalty based on matchability by incorporating the IoU between matched queries and targets with classification confidence.
MAL performs similarly to VFL for high-quality matches but places greater emphasis on low-quality matches, improving the utility of limited positive samples during training.

experiments.summary: DEIM is added on top of RT-DETRv2 and D-FINE and evaluated on COCO val2017 (plus CrowdHuman and Object365 fine-tuning), comparing AP, AP50/75, small/medium/large AP, latency and training cost against YOLOv8/9/10/11 and DETR baselines.

evidence.quote: When integrated with RT-DETR and D-FINE, it consistently boosts performance while reducing training time by 50%.
DEIM-D-FINE-X achieving 54.7% and 56.5% AP at 124 and 78 FPS on an NVIDIA T4 GPU, respectively, without the need for additional data.

When compared directly to YOLOv11-X [13], our DEIM-D-FINE-L outperforms this SoTA model, achieving slightly higher performance (54.7 vs. 54.1 AP) and reducing inference time by 20% (8.07 ms vs. 10.74 ms).
DEIM reduces training time by half and increases AP by 0.5 and 0.9 on RT-DETRv2 [24] with ResNet-50 [14] and ResNet-101 [14] backbones, respectively.

limitations.summary: DEIM's small-object AP still trails some YOLO models within the DETR architecture, and Dense O2O quality degrades if too many objects are packed into each image.
items: Small-object AP remains slightly below YOLO models despite gains over other DETR-based detectors.
Pushing the average object count per image to ~50 hurts performance, likely from positive/negative imbalance and distribution shift.
Benefits are demonstrated mainly on COCO-style detection benchmarks, with CrowdHuman and Object365 as the only extra datasets.

evidence.quote: Despite significant improvements in small object detection over other DETR-based models, our approach shows a slight decrease in small object AP compared to YOLO models.
This gap underscores the ongoing challenges in small object detection within the DETR architecture and suggests potential areas for further improvement.
This decline is likely due to an imbalance in the positive-to-negative ratio and a data distribution shift caused by too many objects.

futureDirections.direction: Explore other techniques beyond mosaic and mixup for raising target counts during training.
futureDirections.quote: their effectiveness suggests further potential for exploring other methods to augment target counts during training.

futureDirections.direction: Refine DEIM and apply it to other high-performance detection tasks.
futureDirections.quote: with the potential for further refinement and application across other high-performance detection tasks.

equations.name: O2M supervision loss
equations.expr: loss = sum_i sum_j f(y_hat_ij, y_i), i=0..N, j=0..Mi

equations.name: Varifocal Loss
equations.expr: VFL(p,q,y): q>0 -> -q(q log p + (1-q) log(1-p)); q=0 -> -alpha p^gamma log(1-p)

equations.name: Matchability-Aware Loss (MAL)
equations.expr: MAL(p,q,y): y=1 -> -q^gamma log p - (1-q^gamma) log(1-p); y=0 -> -p^gamma log(1-p)

applications.detail: Cited as a standard application area for object detection.
applications.quote: widely applied in fields like autonomous driving [5, 6], robot navigation [9], etc.

deploymentClaims: DEIM-D-FINE-L and DEIM-D-FINE-X reach 54.7% and 56.5% AP at 124 and 78 FPS on an NVIDIA T4 GPU.
DEIM-D-FINE-L cuts inference time 20% vs YOLOv11-X (8.07 ms vs 10.74 ms).
A ResNet50-based DETR trained with DEIM reaches 53.2% mAP in a single day (~24 epochs) on one NVIDIA 4090 GPU.
Per-epoch training cost is essentially unchanged (1.183 vs 1.181 GPU-hours) while converging in 71 vs 85 hours.

evidence.quote: paired with RT-DETRv2, DEIM achieves 53.2% AP in a single day of training on an NVIDIA 4090 GPU.
We believe DEIM sets a new baseline for advancements in real-time object detection.
